newsitem.title: USA: War of words escalates on U.S. budget deal.
newsitem.headline: War of words escalates on U.S. budget deal.

text.p: The war of words escalated Thursday over the outlook for a budget deal as the chairman of the Senate Budget Committee said he felt chances of negotiating an agreement with the White House were finished.
"I believe a chance of getting a negotiated budget between the Republicans and the president are finished," Sen. Pete Domenici, a New Mexico Republican, said.
Domenici, at an Appropriations panel hearing, complained that the White House talked more about plans to increase spending than about cuts.

Public statements of bipartisan goodwill that started the year have eroded recently, with each party taking shots at the other over lack of visible progress on the budget. Contentious budget negotiations in the last Congress forced two government shutdowns.
Senate Democratic leaders accused Republicans of stalling on budget talks and failing to formulate their own version.
"The Republicans don't have a plan, they only appear to want to criticize the Democrats' plan," Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota said.
Congressional leaders have been talking privately with administration officials about budget issues, but full-fledged budget negotiations have yet to start.
The White House said it was ready for negotiations to begin. "We're ready to talk now," Lawrence Haas, spokesman for the White House Office of Management and Budget, said.
"We're waiting for the other side to either sit down with us or present an alternative, but the time for carping, it seems to us, is over and the time to work has arrived," he said.

Domenici said Republicans would do a budget: "Just be patient, we'll do one. I'll guarantee that when we're finished it's not going to be a pleasant life for the president, and all these programs he wants," he said.
Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott said Clinton's "unwillingness" to address the consumer price index (CPI) issue "has made it very tough for us to get a budget agreement of any kind."

An advisory commission last December said the CPI overstated inflation by about 1.1 percentage points a year. Federal benefits programs such as Social Security and veterans benefits use the CPI to calculate annual increases, so a lower index could mean big reductions in spending.
"He did not send us a budget that showed courage and leadership, and now he has not been willing to face up to the CPI problem, he's only got one strike left," Lott said.

Republicans are now likely to develop their own budget plan, the Mississippi Republican said. "If he (Clinton) doesn't get engaged with us he will become basically irrelevant in the process and we have to move on," Lott said.
He said it was unlikely the April 15 deadline would be met for a budget resolution, essentially a blueprint for the budget. House Republicans have pegged it to May.
Democrat Senate leader Daschle said Republicans had found a number of excuses for not moving ahead on talks, the latest being discussion on how to make the CPI more accurate.

House Appropriations Committee Chairman Bob Livingston, a Republican from Louisiana, said he was "disappointed" with a list of 254 programs that would be terminated under Clinton's budget. "It is not a serious document," he said about the list from the White House budget office.
"What I have been given is a hodgepodge of small programs, all of which were agreed to by the White House last September as part of our budget agreement," Livingston said.
He called on Clinton to work with Republicans in a "far more constructive, meaningful way to balance the budget. We are off to a poor start."
If Republicans do not like the specifics of Clinton's budget, they should tell the White House what they would change and how they would pay for it, Haas said.

House Budget Committee Chairman John Kasich has said all along it would be a difficult process to reach a budget deal, despite a "false sense" among some people that there would be a budget deal by Easter, the Ohio Republican's spokesman said. "Has anything happened to change his opinion on that? No," the spokesman said.
